Embryonated eggs of the Anhinga (Anhinga anhinga) undergo development at a specific thermal regime; eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after roughly 28 days [ab = roughly 28 days]. This incubation period is typical for a large-bodied waterbird and likely reflects the energetic constraints of maintaining a stable nest temperature in subtropical environments. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are notably small, with a wet weight at birth of only 35 grams [Wwb = 35 grams]. This modest neonatal mass contrasts sharply with the substantial adult sizes the chicks will eventually attain, representing a tiny fraction of the 1226.5 to 1250 gram (1226.5-1250 grams) [Wwi = 1226.5-1250 grams] ultimate body mass characteristic of adults. The transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to an exotrophic chick is a critical phase, and the 28-day (28 days) [ab = 28 days] developmental period at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] may represent an evolutionary compromise between rapid development and the need for sufficiently mature organ systems at hatching. During the first days post-hatch, the altricial nestlings rely entirely on parental provisioning, and their small birth mass necessitates frequent feeding bouts to sustain their rapid growth trajectory. This accelerated growth phase is energetically demanding for the provisioning adults, who must forage intensively to meet the demands of the brood.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, birds maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C] exhibit a resting metabolic rate of 574.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 574.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This oxygen consumption value represents the maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for the species, a relatively elevated metabolic demand consistent with that of a large-bodied, fish-eating piscivore that must maintain high body temperatures while diving. The cost of thermoregulation in water, combined with the energy required for efficient digestion of a protein-rich diet, likely contributes to this substantial metabolic expenditure. In comparative terms, this measured resting oxygen consumption at 40 °C [T = 40 °C] is similar to values reported for other members of the Anhingidae family, though it is modestly higher than that of some similarly sized herons, possibly reflecting the Anhinga's more active underwater pursuit strategy. The metabolic data were obtained from respirometry trials on captive individuals, ensuring that the measurements reflect true basal conditions rather than activity-related elevations. These energetic constraints have clear implications for the species' overall life history strategy, influencing everything from foraging time budgets to the allocation of resources toward reproduction.

Reproductive output in Anhinga anhinga follows a pattern closely tied to the thermal environment. At a body temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is realized through a seasonal breeding strategy where females lay between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch], producing a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive output of 4 offspring per year [Ri = 4 offspring per year]. This annual reproductive effort is constrained by the long developmental period required for the altricial chicks to reach independence. The time since birth at first brood is approximately 730 days [tR = approximately 730 days] when individuals are maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], indicating that the first breeding event is delayed until the second year of life. This deferred reproduction, relative to smaller waterbirds, likely reflects the time required to attain the substantial body size necessary for successful nesting and chick provisioning. The individual milestones leading to this first reproduction event are tightly orchestrated: puberty is reached relatively early in the developmental sequence.

Sexual maturation in Anhinga anhinga occurs several months before the first breeding attempt, a pattern common among species with extended parental care requirements. Under the thermal conditions associated with active metabolic function at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 180 days [tp = approximately 180 days]. This indicates that gonadal development and the onset of gametogenesis are completed by around six months of age, yet the actual initiation of reproductive activity is deferred for approximately another year and a half until the 730-day (730 days since birth) [tR = 730 days since birth] point at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. The intervening period is likely devoted to completing skeletal growth, refining foraging skills, and establishing a territory or a position within the social hierarchy that permits successful breeding. Young individuals also undergo a critical developmental transition during the nestling and fledgling phase; fledging, the point at which a chick achieves its first sustained flight, occurs at 42 days after hatching [tx = 42 days after hatching] when maintained at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively extended fledging period, typical of altricial waterbirds, allows for the full development of the flight feathers and the musculature required for proficient aerial and underwater locomotion.

The ultimate body mass attained by adults exhibits clear sexual dimorphism in Anhinga anhinga, a trait common among many waterbirds where males are typically larger. The maximum adult wet weight recorded for females is 1226.5 grams [Wwi = 1226.5 grams], while males achieve a slightly greater ultimate wet weight of 1250 grams [Wwi = 1250 grams]. This modest size difference, approximately 2 percent, is less pronounced than that observed in some diving ducks but is consistent with the monogamous breeding system and shared parental duties typical of the Anhingidae. The substantial increase in mass from the 35-gram (35 grams) [Wwb = 35 grams] neonatal value to these adult masses represents a remarkable growth factor of over 35-fold, underscoring the intensity of the altricial growth phase. In terms of total longevity, available data indicate that the maximum lifespan for this species, recorded under conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is approximately 16.4 years [am = approximately 16.4 years]. This relatively long life expectancy, comparable to that of other large piscivorous waterbirds, is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high annual fecundity. With a single annual clutch of 1 to 5 eggs, the lifetime reproductive output can accumulate over 16.4 years, making each breeding season a valuable opportunity for a long-lived species like the Anhinga.
